prompt: Which cranial nerve is most directly responsible for tongue movement during speech and swallowing?
choices: The hypoglossal nerve, cranial nerve XII.
The optic nerve, cranial nerve II.
The vestibulocochlear nerve, cranial nerve VIII.
The accessory nerve, cranial nerve XI.
rationale: Cranial nerve XII supplies the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, so weakness can affect articulation and bolus control.
choiceRationales: Correct. Cranial nerve XII supplies the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, so weakness can affect articulation and bolus control.
The optic nerve carries visual information from the retina and has no motor role in tongue movement for articulation or bolus control.
The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance information, so it does not innervate the tongue muscles used in speech and swallowing.
The accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles and part of the palate, not the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles.

prompt: Which cranial nerve provides major motor innervation to the muscles of expression across the brow, cheek, and lips?
choices: The trigeminal nerve, cranial nerve V.
The facial nerve, cranial nerve VII.
The glossopharyngeal nerve, cranial nerve IX.
The vagus nerve, cranial nerve X.
rationale: Cranial nerve VII supplies the muscles of facial expression and contributes to lip closure and facial symmetry. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: The trigeminal nerve provides facial sensation and motor control of the jaw for chewing, but it does not drive the muscles of facial expression.

Correct. Cranial nerve VII supplies the muscles of facial expression and contributes to lip closure and facial symmetry. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
The glossopharyngeal nerve contributes to taste, pharyngeal sensation, and stylopharyngeus function rather than to the muscles of facial expression.
The vagus nerve supplies laryngeal, pharyngeal, and velar muscles, so it supports phonation and swallowing rather than facial expression.

prompt: What aerodynamic condition is generally required to initiate and sustain voiced phonation?
choices: Complete absence of airflow through the glottis while the vocal folds remain fully abducted throughout speech.
Continuous elevation of the soft palate while the vocal folds stay apart during the entire spoken utterance.
Adequate respiratory support and subglottal pressure that sets the adducted vocal folds into vibration.
Maximal tongue-base retraction held throughout the utterance to narrow the pharynx and create vocal resonance.
rationale: Voice depends on coordinated respiration, phonation, and resonance; airflow and pressure interact with vocal-fold position and tissue properties.
choiceRationales: Voicing requires airflow and pressure beneath adducted folds, so an absence of glottal airflow with abducted folds cannot produce phonation.
Velar elevation shapes oral versus nasal resonance, but without vocal-fold adduction the airstream does not generate voiced phonation.
Correct. Voice depends on coordinated respiration, phonation, and resonance; airflow and pressure interact with vocal-fold position and tissue properties.
Tongue-base retraction changes pharyngeal resonance and can add strain, but it does not supply the subglottal pressure needed to initiate voicing.

prompt: What is the primary speech consequence of velopharyngeal insufficiency?
choices: A primarily receptive-language impairment that limits understanding of complex spoken sentences and directions.
A bilateral sensorineural hearing loss caused by damage to the cochlea that affects perception of speech sounds.
An isolated word-finding difficulty in which the speaker cannot retrieve familiar nouns during conversation.
Excessive nasal resonance and reduced intraoral pressure for pressure consonants such as stops and fricatives.
rationale: The velopharyngeal valve directs acoustic energy and oral air pressure; incomplete closure can cause hypernasality and nasal air emission.
choiceRationales: Velopharyngeal insufficiency is a structural problem with closing the nasal port, so it affects resonance and pressure rather than language comprehension.
Sensorineural hearing loss arises in the cochlea or auditory nerve and is not caused by incomplete velopharyngeal closure during speech.
Word-finding difficulty is a lexical retrieval problem, whereas velopharyngeal insufficiency produces hypernasality and weak pressure consonants.
Correct. The velopharyngeal valve directs acoustic energy and oral air pressure; incomplete closure can cause hypernasality and nasal air emission.

prompt: Which observation is most consistent with typical early communication development?
choices: Joint attention, turn taking, gesture, and varied babble develop before and alongside first words.
Reading comprehension consistently develops before joint attention and gestural communication in most toddlers.
Complex sentence syntax normally appears before infants begin using intentional gestures such as pointing.
Phonological awareness is fully mature during canonical babbling, before the child produces any first words.
rationale: Prelinguistic social interaction, gesture, vocal play, and babbling provide foundations for later speech and language. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Correct. Prelinguistic social interaction, gesture, vocal play, and babbling provide foundations for later speech and language. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
Reading comprehension emerges years after early prelinguistic skills, so it cannot precede joint attention and gesture in typical development.
Intentional gestures such as pointing typically appear before first words, and complex syntax develops much later in the preschool years.
Phonological awareness continues developing into the early school years and is not mature during the canonical babbling stage of infancy.

prompt: Which language component concerns word meanings and relationships among concepts?
choices: Phonotactics.
Semantics.
Prosody only.
Respiration.
rationale: Semantics addresses word and sentence meaning, including vocabulary, concepts, categories, and lexical relationships. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Phonotactics describes the permissible sequences of sounds in a language, which is a phonological rather than a meaning-based component.

Correct. Semantics addresses word and sentence meaning, including vocabulary, concepts, categories, and lexical relationships. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
Prosody concerns stress, rhythm, and intonation patterns, which can signal meaning but do not define word meanings and conceptual relations.
Respiration is a physiological subsystem that supports speech production rather than a component of language describing meaning.

prompt: Which statement best describes neuroplasticity after acquired brain injury?
choices: Damaged neural tissue returns to its exact premorbid structure once the acute medical phase of recovery has ended.
Practice and therapy have little influence on neural reorganization after the acute phase of recovery has ended.
Neural systems can reorganize with experience, though recovery depends on lesion, timing, intensity, and health.
Recovery after brain injury is determined mainly by chronological age, regardless of lesion site or practice.
rationale: Experience-dependent change supports rehabilitation, but prognosis must account for multiple person, injury, task, and environmental variables.
choiceRationales: Neuroplasticity involves reorganization and compensation rather than an exact return to the premorbid state of damaged neural tissue.
Experience-dependent practice continues to influence recovery in later phases, which is why intensity and task relevance matter in treatment.
Correct. Experience-dependent change supports rehabilitation, but prognosis must account for multiple person, injury, task, and environmental variables.
Age is one factor, but lesion characteristics, timing, health, and the amount and relevance of practice also shape recovery outcomes.

prompt: How does prevalence differ from incidence?
choices: Prevalence is a reliability coefficient for test scores, while incidence is a validity coefficient for diagnoses.
Prevalence counts only resolved cases in a population, while incidence counts every case diagnosed in the past.
Incidence describes all existing cases in a population at once, without regard to any particular time period.
Prevalence counts existing cases in a population; incidence counts new cases over a specified period.
rationale: Prevalence and incidence answer different epidemiologic questions and should not be substituted for one another. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Reliability and validity are measurement properties of assessments, whereas prevalence and incidence are epidemiological counts of cases.
Prevalence includes all existing cases at a given time, not only resolved cases, so this description reverses its meaning.
Incidence specifically counts new cases arising during a defined period, which distinguishes it from prevalence of existing cases.

Correct. Prevalence and incidence answer different epidemiologic questions and should not be substituted for one another. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.

prompt: A hearing loss caused by reduced sound transmission through the outer or middle ear is classified as what type?
choices: Conductive hearing loss.
Central auditory processing disorder by definition.
Sensorineural hearing loss.
Functional aphonia.
rationale: Conductive loss involves sound transmission through the outer or middle ear; sensorineural loss involves cochlear or auditory-nerve function.
choiceRationales: Correct. Conductive loss involves sound transmission through the outer or middle ear; sensorineural loss involves cochlear or auditory-nerve function.
Disorders of auditory processing arise within the central auditory system and involve how sound is interpreted, not reduced transmission through the outer or middle ear.
Damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve defines a sensorineural loss, whereas reduced transmission through the outer or middle ear defines conductive loss.
Functional aphonia is a voice disorder without structural cause and has no relationship to how sound travels through the ear.

prompt: Before initiating a nonemergency evaluation or treatment, what should informed consent include?
choices: A signed consent form obtained at check-in before the clinician explains the planned evaluation or treatment.
The nature, purpose, benefits, material risks, alternatives, and limits, with a voluntary chance to decide.
A written guarantee that the recommended treatment will succeed if the client attends every scheduled session.
A description of the clinician’s single preferred option, so the client is not confused by alternative approaches.
rationale: Consent is an ongoing communication process, not merely a form, and requirements vary with setting, law, capacity, and service.
choiceRationales: A signature obtained before explanation is not informed consent, because the person has not yet received the information needed to decide.
Correct. Consent is an ongoing communication process, not merely a form, and requirements vary with setting, law, capacity, and service.
Clinicians cannot guarantee outcomes, and promising success misrepresents risks and benefits that consent discussions must convey honestly.
Informed consent requires discussing reasonable alternatives, so presenting only the preferred option prevents a genuinely informed choice.

prompt: An SLP is asked to use an unfamiliar instrumental procedure without adequate preparation. What is the best response?
choices: Proceed with the procedure because the equipment software produces an automatic score that requires little judgment.
Ask a speech-language pathology assistant to perform the procedure independently while the SLP reviews results later.
Seek qualified training and supervision, collaborate or refer as needed, and avoid practicing beyond competence.
Use the procedure as requested and omit its limitations from the report so the referring team receives clear answers.
rationale: Ethical practice requires competence based on education, training, experience, and appropriate consultation or referral.
choiceRationales: Automated software scores do not replace clinical competence, and interpreting instrumental findings requires appropriate training and judgment.
Delegating an unfamiliar procedure to an assistant without oversight violates supervision requirements and compounds the competence problem.
Correct. Ethical practice requires competence based on education, training, experience, and appropriate consultation or referral.
Omitting limitations misrepresents the quality of findings and violates ethical duties of honest, accurate reporting to the team.

prompt: Which privacy framework should an SLP apply when sharing records?
choices: Assume HIPAA applies identically in every school setting and follow hospital release procedures for all records.
Assume FERPA permits any school employee to access student records whenever they have a professional question.
Share the complete clinical record whenever another licensed professional asks so collaboration stays efficient.
Identify the governing law and policy, verify authority and purpose, obtain needed consent, and share securely.
rationale: FERPA, HIPAA, state law, consent, and organizational policy can apply differently; employment alone does not create unlimited access.
choiceRationales: Schools are often governed by FERPA rather than HIPAA, so assuming HIPAA applies identically can lead to incorrect disclosure decisions.
FERPA limits access to school officials with a legitimate educational interest, so it does not permit access by every employee.
Disclosure should be limited to authorized information for a specific purpose, so sharing the full record on request exceeds what is permitted.
Correct. FERPA, HIPAA, state law, consent, and organizational policy can apply differently; employment alone does not create unlimited access.

prompt: What makes clinical documentation defensible?
choices: Objective, timely notes on status, procedures, response, data, interpretation, plan, and communication.
A note copied from the previous session that does not reflect what actually occurred during today’s treatment.
A brief statement that the client did well today, written without data, interpretation, or a follow-up plan.
A billing code entered for the visit without any clinical information describing services or client response.
rationale: Documentation should accurately represent services and decisions while protecting privacy and meeting applicable legal and organizational requirements.
choiceRationales: Correct. Documentation should accurately represent services and decisions while protecting privacy and meeting applicable legal and organizational requirements.
Copied notes misrepresent the session and can constitute fraudulent documentation, so they are not defensible clinical records.
Vague statements lack the objective data and interpretation needed to justify services and track progress over time.
Billing codes indicate service type for payment but do not document clinical status, procedures, response, or the plan of care.

prompt: An SLP has a financial relationship with a company whose device is being recommended. What should the SLP do?
choices: Keep the financial relationship private because the device may genuinely help the client communicate effectively.
Disclose the conflict, keep feature matching and alternatives objective, and follow ethics and organizational policy.
Recommend the highest-priced device option so the client receives the most advanced features available on the market.
Let the device vendor determine the client’s candidacy because company staff know the product features best.
rationale: Transparency and independent clinical judgment protect the individual from exploitation and support informed choice. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Even if the device may help, hiding a financial relationship violates ethics requirements and undermines trust in the recommendation.

Correct. Transparency and independent clinical judgment protect the individual from exploitation and support informed choice. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
Price does not indicate fit, and AAC decisions should be based on objective matching of needs and features rather than cost alone.
Vendors have a financial interest, so candidacy decisions must remain with qualified clinicians using objective assessment evidence.

prompt: What must an SLP do when supervising an assistant or student clinician?
choices: The assistant assumes independent responsibility for diagnosis once they complete the initial training period.
The client’s family becomes responsible for the quality of services delivered by the student clinician or assistant.
Match tasks to competence, provide required direction and observation, and keep responsibility under current rules.
Supervision becomes unnecessary after the student clinician completes one successful session without any errors.
rationale: Delegation does not transfer professional accountability; requirements depend on credentials, scope, setting, and jurisdiction.
choiceRationales: Assistants cannot diagnose; diagnostic responsibility remains with the certified SLP regardless of how much training the assistant has completed.
Families are partners in care but are not responsible for clinical quality, which remains the supervising clinician’s obligation.
Correct. Delegation does not transfer professional accountability; requirements depend on credentials, scope, setting, and jurisdiction.
One successful session does not establish competence, and supervision requirements continue according to the current regulations that apply.

prompt: Before providing telepractice across a jurisdictional boundary, what should an SLP verify?
choices: The clinician’s home-state license only, since telepractice sessions are conducted from the clinician’s own office.
Whether the selected video platform has attractive graphics and engaging features that keep clients motivated.
Whether telepractice removes the need for local emergency planning because sessions occur over a secure network.
Licensure rules where the client is located, consent, privacy, emergency procedures, technology, and appropriateness.
rationale: Telepractice remains clinical practice and requires jurisdictional authority, privacy safeguards, accessibility, contingency planning, and appropriate care.
choiceRationales: Licensure requirements are typically tied to where the client is located, so a home-state license alone may not authorize cross-boundary services.
Visual appeal does not address the privacy, security, and clinical appropriateness requirements that govern telepractice decisions.
Remote services still require a plan for emergencies at the client’s location, so local emergency procedures remain essential.
Correct. Telepractice remains clinical practice and requires jurisdictional authority, privacy safeguards, accessibility, contingency planning, and appropriate care.

prompt: In a school, what is the key distinction between a medical diagnosis and IDEA service eligibility?
choices: Whether disability and educational impact meet criteria and require specially designed instruction via the team.
A medical diagnosis from a physician determines the IEP services the school must provide to the student.
School eligibility for speech-language services can be decided by the speech-language pathologist alone.
Educational performance refers only to report-card grades, so students earning passing grades cannot qualify.
rationale: Clinical diagnosis and educational eligibility serve different legal purposes; teams must follow current federal, state, and local criteria.
choiceRationales: Correct. Clinical diagnosis and educational eligibility serve different legal purposes; teams must follow current federal, state, and local criteria.
A medical diagnosis can inform the team, but IDEA eligibility requires meeting educational criteria through the team process.
Eligibility is a multidisciplinary team decision with parent participation, not a determination made by one professional alone.
Educational performance includes functional and social communication, so passing grades do not by themselves rule out eligibility.

prompt: What is the strongest interprofessional response when swallowing, respiratory, nutritional, and communication needs overlap?
choices: Have each discipline manage its own decisions independently so professional responsibilities stay clearly separated.
Share scope-relevant findings, clarify roles, coordinate goals and safety, honor priorities, and refer as needed.
Avoid interprofessional collaboration to preserve professional autonomy and prevent conflicting recommendations.
Defer all communication and swallowing decisions to another discipline that has broader medical responsibility.
rationale: Team-based care integrates distinct expertise while preserving scope, accountability, shared decision making, and continuity.
choiceRationales: Overlapping needs require coordinated plans, and separate independent decisions risk conflicting recommendations and gaps in safety planning.
Correct. Team-based care integrates distinct expertise while preserving scope, accountability, shared decision making, and continuity.
Avoiding collaboration undermines safe, coordinated care in situations when respiratory, nutritional, swallowing, and communication needs interact.
SLPs hold specific expertise in communication and swallowing, so deferring all such decisions abandons responsibility within scope.

prompt: Which elements make up evidence-based practice in speech-language pathology?
choices: Published research findings alone, applied to each client regardless of fit with their needs or circumstances.
The clinician’s established habits and favorite techniques developed through years of successful clinical practice.
Best available research, clinical expertise, and the person’s values, preferences, culture, and goals.
A family preference adopted without providing information about the likely benefits and risks of each option.
rationale: Evidence-based practice integrates multiple sources through shared decision making rather than treating any single source as sufficient.
choiceRationales: Research is one component, but evidence-based practice also integrates clinical expertise and the individual’s values and circumstances.
Clinical experience matters, yet habit alone ignores research evidence and client perspectives that evidence-based practice requires.
Correct. Evidence-based practice integrates multiple sources through shared decision making rather than treating any single source as sufficient.
Client preferences are central, but they should be informed by information about benefits and risks rather than adopted without discussion.

prompt: What is the purpose of a PICO question?
choices: To list just the client’s diagnosis and the clinician’s preferred standardized test for the next evaluation.
To replace measurement of treatment outcomes with expert opinion from experienced colleagues in the field.
To guarantee that a single published study will answer every clinical question that arises for a given case.
To specify the population or problem, intervention, comparison when relevant, and the outcome of interest.
rationale: PICO helps focus searching and appraisal by connecting a defined population, intervention, comparison, and meaningful outcome.
choiceRationales: A PICO question structures a searchable clinical question, which requires more than a diagnosis and a preferred assessment tool.
PICO explicitly includes an outcome so evidence can be evaluated; it does not replace outcome measurement with opinion.
PICO focuses a literature search but cannot guarantee that any single study will answer all questions about a particular client.
Correct. PICO helps focus searching and appraisal by connecting a defined population, intervention, comparison, and meaningful outcome.

prompt: Which study design best supports a causal claim about an intervention when feasible and ethical?
choices: A well-conducted randomized controlled trial with valid outcomes, fidelity monitoring, and sound analysis.
An uncontrolled testimonial from a satisfied client describing improvement after receiving the intervention.
A cross-sectional prevalence survey describing how many clinicians currently use the intervention in practice.
A single case history without repeated measurement, baseline data, or comparison to other treatment conditions.
rationale: Random assignment can strengthen causal inference, but attrition, implementation, measurement, applicability, and ethics still require appraisal.
choiceRationales: Correct. Random assignment can strengthen causal inference, but attrition, implementation, measurement, applicability, and ethics still require appraisal.
Testimonials lack controls and are vulnerable to bias, so they cannot establish that an intervention caused the reported change.
Prevalence surveys describe how common a practice is, not whether the intervention causes improved outcomes for clients.
Without repeated measurement or comparison, a case history cannot rule out maturation or other explanations for change.

prompt: A measure produces highly consistent scores but does not assess the intended construct. How should it be described?
choices: The measure is valid because highly consistent scores show that it accurately captures the intended construct.
The measure may be reliable but lacks validity evidence for the intended interpretation and use.
The measure is valid because it is standardized and administered under the same conditions for every client.
Score consistency makes a clear construct definition unnecessary when selecting the measure for evaluation.
rationale: Reliability concerns precision; validity concerns evidence supporting a particular interpretation and decision in context.
choiceRationales: Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; consistent scores can still measure something other than the intended construct.
Correct. Reliability concerns precision; validity concerns evidence supporting a particular interpretation and decision in context.
Standardized administration improves consistency, but it does not demonstrate that the scores support the intended interpretation.
A clear construct definition is essential for judging validity, regardless of how consistent the scores appear across administrations.

prompt: Why should effect size and confidence intervals accompany a statistical-significance result?
choices: They confirm that statistical significance guarantees a meaningful benefit for every client receiving treatment.
They allow clinicians to set aside uncertainty once the p value falls below the conventional significance level.
They show magnitude, precision, and practical importance, alongside study quality and relevance to the person.
They show that the average treatment effect applies identically to every participant included in the study.
rationale: Statistical significance alone does not establish clinical importance, precision, causality, applicability, or individual response.
choiceRationales: Statistical significance indicates an effect is unlikely to be zero but does not establish that the benefit is clinically meaningful.
Confidence intervals communicate uncertainty, which remains important even when a p value crosses a significance threshold.
Correct. Statistical significance alone does not establish clinical importance, precision, causality, applicability, or individual response.
Average effects mask individual variability, so clinicians must consider how results apply to the specific person being served.

prompt: What is a major purpose of dynamic assessment with a multilingual learner?
choices: Whether an English-normed standard score alone establishes a language disorder for the multilingual learner.
Whether the learner can imitate the examiner’s accent accurately during structured repetition activities.
Whether bilingual language use at home should be discontinued so the learner can focus on learning English.
How the learner responds to mediated support, helping separate limited opportunity and difference from disorder.
rationale: Dynamic assessment examines learning processes and response to support and complements history, language samples, observation, and other evidence.
choiceRationales: English-normed scores often misrepresent multilingual learners, which is why dynamic assessment examines response to teaching instead.
Accent imitation is unrelated to language learning ability and does not help distinguish difference from disorder.
Dynamic assessment does not aim to discontinue bilingualism, which supports development and should be valued as a strength.
Correct. Dynamic assessment examines learning processes and response to support and complements history, language samples, observation, and other evidence.

prompt: When a trained interpreter is needed, which practice is strongest?
choices: Brief the interpreter, address the client directly, document adaptations, and debrief about observations.
Use a young family member as interpreter for convenience during a high-stakes diagnostic evaluation session.
Ask the trained interpreter to determine whether the client’s language patterns indicate a communication disorder.
Report standardized scores as unchanged after translating test items without validation for the client’s language.
rationale: Qualified collaboration preserves roles, access, privacy, and interpretive caution; translation can alter standardization and score meaning.
choiceRationales: Correct. Qualified collaboration preserves roles, access, privacy, and interpretive caution; translation can alter standardization and score meaning.
Young family members lack training and impartiality and may face role strain, so they are inappropriate for high-stakes evaluations.
Interpreters provide linguistic and cultural information, but diagnostic decisions remain the responsibility of the qualified clinician.
Unvalidated translation changes item difficulty and invalidates norms, so standardized scores cannot be reported as unchanged.

prompt: A multilingual child uses forms consistent with the home-language system and learns age-expected patterns across languages. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Any departure from mainstream English patterns proves that the child has a communication disorder needing services.
The pattern may reflect linguistic difference; disorder needs evidence not explained by exposure or dialect.
A low score on an English-only standardized test is sufficient to diagnose a language disorder in this child.
Strengths observed in the child’s home language should be excluded from the evaluation to keep scoring consistent.
rationale: Culturally and linguistically responsive assessment considers all languages, dialects, opportunity, community norms, and response to support.
choiceRationales: Features consistent with the home language or dialect reflect difference, not disorder, so departures from mainstream English are not proof.
Correct. Culturally and linguistically responsive assessment considers all languages, dialects, opportunity, community norms, and response to support.
Scores from English-only testing are biased for multilingual children and cannot by themselves establish a language disorder.
Home-language strengths are essential evidence for distinguishing difference from disorder and must be included in the evaluation.

prompt: A child consistently substitutes stops for fricatives across many words. What does this profile most directly represent?
choices: A receptive-language disorder that alone explains the substitutions without considering speech-sound patterns.
A vocal-fold lesion that disrupts airflow needed to produce continuous fricative sounds during connected speech.
A phonological stopping pattern, interpreted with age, language, dialect, stimulability, and intelligibility.
A pharyngeal swallowing impairment that limits the oral pressure the child needs for producing fricative sounds.
rationale: A systematic class-based sound change is phonological; diagnosis requires broader developmental, linguistic, motor, hearing, and functional evidence.
choiceRationales: Systematic substitutions of stops for fricatives describe a phonological pattern in speech, not a deficit in receptive-language comprehension.
Vocal-fold lesions affect voice quality rather than producing consistent substitution of stops for fricatives across many words.
Correct. A systematic class-based sound change is phonological; diagnosis requires broader developmental, linguistic, motor, hearing, and functional evidence.
Swallowing impairments involve bolus transport and airway protection, not the phonological rule of substituting stops for fricatives.

prompt: Which feature most distinguishes stuttering from typical disfluency?
choices: Word-finding pauses during conversation, which by themselves establish a diagnosis of developmental stuttering.
The total syllable count in a speech sample, which is the only factor needed to distinguish stuttering from typical speech.
Listener discomfort during conversation, which is sufficient by itself to diagnose stuttering in the speaker.
Stuttering-like disfluencies with tension or impact, assessed for frequency, context, experience, and participation.
rationale: Fluency assessment includes overt behaviors, secondary behaviors, anticipation, avoidance, emotional impact, communication participation, and the speaker’s goals.
choiceRationales: Word-finding pauses can occur in typical speech and language disorders, so they do not establish stuttering on their own.
Syllable counts help quantify disfluency, but type, tension, and the speaker’s experience are needed to distinguish stuttering.
Listener reactions are subjective and do not capture the disfluency types or speaker impact that define stuttering.
Correct. Fluency assessment includes overt behaviors, secondary behaviors, anticipation, avoidance, emotional impact, communication participation, and the speaker’s goals.

prompt: Which contrast best differentiates dysarthria from apraxia of speech?
choices: Dysarthria reflects impaired neuromuscular execution, while apraxia mainly affects motor planning and programming.
Both dysarthria and apraxia of speech are primarily language-comprehension disorders affecting understanding of speech.
Apraxia of speech is caused by muscle weakness in the lips and tongue that limits strength during speech production.
Dysarthria affects the motor control of handwriting and typing but leaves speech production fully intact.
rationale: Motor-speech differential diagnosis integrates strength, tone, coordination, consistency, prosody, articulation, phonation, respiration, and neurologic findings.
choiceRationales: Correct. Motor-speech differential diagnosis integrates strength, tone, coordination, consistency, prosody, articulation, phonation, respiration, and neurologic findings.
Both are motor speech disorders, so describing them as comprehension disorders confuses them with receptive language impairments.
Apraxia of speech involves planning and programming deficits rather than weakness, which is more characteristic of dysarthria.
Dysarthria specifically affects speech subsystems such as respiration, phonation, and articulation, and it is not defined by handwriting difficulty.

prompt: After a left-hemisphere stroke, a client has impaired word retrieval, sentence formulation, and comprehension. What broad disorder is most likely?
choices: Developmental phonological disorder.
Aphasia.
Isolated conductive hearing loss.
Velopharyngeal insufficiency.
rationale: Aphasia is an acquired language disorder that can affect speaking, listening, reading, and writing in varying patterns and severities.
choiceRationales: A phonological disorder of developmental origin begins in childhood and does not explain new word-retrieval and comprehension deficits after stroke.
Correct. Aphasia is an acquired language disorder that can affect speaking, listening, reading, and writing in varying patterns and severities.
Problems with sound transmission through the outer or middle ear would not produce impaired sentence formulation or word retrieval.
Incomplete velopharyngeal closure affects resonance and pressure consonants rather than causing deficits in word retrieval and language comprehension.

prompt: Which feature is especially important in cognitive-communication disorders after traumatic brain injury?
choices: Normal articulation and fluency after traumatic brain injury rule out any communication disability for the person.
Confrontation naming is the one skill that needs assessment when evaluating communication after brain injury.
Breakdowns can arise from attention, memory, executive, self-monitoring, and social-cognition deficits in daily life.
Cognition and communication should be treated as unrelated areas that require entirely separate interventions.
rationale: Cognitive processes support discourse, learning, organization, inference, self-regulation, and participation even when basic speech is intact.
choiceRationales: Cognitive-communication deficits often occur with intact articulation, so normal speech does not rule out functional communication problems.
Naming is only one skill, and cognitive-communication assessment must examine attention, memory, executive function, and discourse.
Correct. Cognitive processes support discourse, learning, organization, inference, self-regulation, and participation even when basic speech is intact.
Cognitive processes directly shape communication after brain injury, so treating them as unrelated misses the source of breakdowns.

prompt: Hypernasality and nasal air emission after cleft-palate repair most directly raise concern about what mechanism?
choices: A semantic-category deficit that limits retrieval of words for specific concepts such as foods or animals.
A behavioral refusal to speak that develops when children feel anxious about speaking in social settings.
An isolated visual impairment that reduces the child’s ability to see and imitate the movements of other speakers.
Velopharyngeal dysfunction, with structural and learned articulation components assessed separately.
rationale: Structural or functional velopharyngeal problems can alter resonance and pressure; compensatory articulations may coexist and require different management.
choiceRationales: Semantic deficits affect word meaning and retrieval, not the resonance and nasal air emission linked to velopharyngeal function.
Hypernasality and nasal air emission are physical signs of velopharyngeal problems rather than evidence of behavioral refusal.
Visual impairment does not cause hypernasality or nasal air emission, which instead reflect incomplete closure of the velopharyngeal port.
Correct. Structural or functional velopharyngeal problems can alter resonance and pressure; compensatory articulations may coexist and require different management.

prompt: Which characteristic is central to social communication assessment?
choices: Pragmatic interaction across natural partners, settings, purposes, and cultural expectations.
Oral-motor strength measured during nonspeech tasks such as tongue protrusion and lip rounding exercises.
Pure-tone hearing thresholds measured across frequencies during a standard audiometric screening procedure.
Accurate definitions of isolated vocabulary words provided by the student during a structured testing session.
rationale: Social communication involves using verbal and nonverbal communication for interaction, adapting to context, and following discourse and conversation expectations.
choiceRationales: Correct. Social communication involves using verbal and nonverbal communication for interaction, adapting to context, and following discourse and conversation expectations.
Oral-motor strength relates to speech production mechanics, not the pragmatic skills used in real social interactions.
Hearing thresholds are relevant background information, but they do not describe how a person uses language socially.
Vocabulary definitions measure semantic knowledge in isolation, whereas evaluating social communication requires observing interaction in context.

prompt: During eating, a patient repeatedly coughs with liquids and develops a wet vocal quality after swallowing. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
choices: A normal response to drinking liquids that rules out dysphagia and does not require further clinical follow-up.
Possible airway invasion or impaired clearance requiring timely evaluation and medical or instrumental referral.
Evidence of an expressive-language disorder that affects the patient’s ability to describe swallowing problems.
Clear proof that aspiration occurs on every swallow, so all oral intake must stop without further assessment.
rationale: Cough and wet voice can be warning signs but do not alone determine physiology; silent aspiration is also possible and assessment guides decisions.
choiceRationales: Repeated coughing with a wet vocal quality is a warning sign of possible airway invasion, so it does not rule out dysphagia.
Correct. Cough and wet voice can be warning signs but do not alone determine physiology; silent aspiration is also possible and assessment guides decisions.
These signs relate to swallowing safety rather than language, so they do not indicate an expressive-language disorder.
Clinical signs suggest risk but cannot confirm aspiration on every swallow, which requires further evaluation to characterize.

prompt: What is the primary purpose of a screening?
choices: Confirming that the student has a communication disorder so that eligibility can be documented at the meeting.
Producing a detailed score profile that can be converted directly into treatment goals and a service schedule.
Identifying possible risk and follow-up need, without by itself establishing a diagnosis or eligibility.
Replacing the case history and full testing so that no additional information needs to be collected later.
rationale: Screening is a brief risk-identification process whose follow-up depends on the tool, result, context, urgency, and governing procedures.
choiceRationales: A screening is brief and designed to flag possible risk; confirming a disorder requires a comprehensive evaluation with multiple sources.
Screening results are too limited to define treatment targets, so goals should follow a fuller assessment of strengths and needs.
Correct. Screening is a brief risk-identification process whose follow-up depends on the tool, result, context, urgency, and governing procedures.
A screen does not replace history or comprehensive assessment; a failed or uncertain result is the reason to gather more information.

prompt: Which case-history information is most useful before selecting assessment procedures?
choices: Chronological age and current grade placement, since these alone determine which standardized battery should be given.
The referring professional’s diagnostic label, which should guide test selection before any other background is gathered.
A single previous test score from the record, which is enough to choose procedures without interviewing the family.
Developmental, medical, sensory, linguistic, cultural, educational, family, and client-priority background details.
rationale: A relevant case history helps define questions, identify risk and protective factors, select accessible procedures, and interpret findings.
choiceRationales: Age and grade help with norm selection, but they say nothing about hearing, language exposure, medical history, or the client’s priorities.
A referral label is a hypothesis to examine, and relying on it first can bias procedure selection and narrow the clinical questions asked.
One earlier score lacks context about conditions, language, and change over time, so it cannot stand in for a full case history.
Correct. A relevant case history helps define questions, identify risk and protective factors, select accessible procedures, and interpret findings.

prompt: How should a failed hearing screening affect a speech-language evaluation?
choices: Arrange timely audiologic follow-up and interpret communication results in light of uncertain auditory access.
Proceed to diagnose a language disorder from the test scores, because hearing status does not change the interpretation.
Repeat the language testing at several later sessions until the standard score rises into the average range.
Treat the screening result as unrelated to communication and document it separately from the language findings.
rationale: Hearing status affects access to speech and language; follow-up and coordinated interpretation are essential. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Correct. Hearing status affects access to speech and language; follow-up and coordinated interpretation are essential. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
Reduced auditory access can depress language scores, so a diagnosis made without resolving the hearing question may be inaccurate.
Retesting until a score improves inflates practice effects and ignores the possibility that hearing is limiting access to the test items.
Hearing directly affects speech perception and language learning, so a failed screen must shape how the communication findings are read.

prompt: What is the strongest basis for selecting a standardized test?
choices: It is the instrument already available in the clinic, so it can be given without ordering or learning a new measure.
It fits the referral question and has adequate reliability, validity, norm, and fairness evidence for the intended use.
It produces an attractive, easy-to-read score report that families and teachers can understand at a quick glance.
It is widely used by other clinicians in the district, regardless of whether its norms match the person being tested.
rationale: Test selection is purpose- and person-specific; standardization does not guarantee validity or fairness for every inference.
choiceRationales: Convenience does not establish that a measure answers the referral question or yields valid scores for this particular person.
Correct. Test selection is purpose- and person-specific; standardization does not guarantee validity or fairness for every inference.
A clear report format may help communication with families, but it says nothing about the psychometric quality of the scores.
Popularity cannot substitute for evidence that the norm sample, content, and accessibility features suit the individual and purpose.

prompt: Why should a confidence interval accompany a standard score?
choices: It identifies the lower bound as the clinically meaningful value that should be reported as the person’s true ability.
It shows that the diagnosis is confirmed whenever the interval falls below the cutoff score used for eligibility.
It conveys measurement error, showing that the obtained score estimates the true score within a range of precision.
It indicates that standard scores are exact trait values, so repeated testing would produce the identical result.
rationale: Confidence intervals communicate uncertainty and help prevent overinterpretation of small or unstable differences. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: The interval describes a plausible range around the obtained score; neither bound should be singled out as the true ability value.
Score precision informs interpretation, but a diagnosis integrates many data sources rather than resting on one interval and cutoff.

Correct. Confidence intervals communicate uncertainty and help prevent overinterpretation of small or unstable differences. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
Every standard score contains measurement error, which is precisely why a confidence band is reported alongside the obtained value.

prompt: What is a major advantage of criterion-referenced assessment?
choices: It yields a diagnostic standard score that ranks the person against a nationally representative norm sample.
It removes the need to document reliability, because criteria are set by the clinician rather than by a publisher.
It ensures that skills mastered on the task will generalize to daily conversation without further probing.
Performance is compared with defined skills or criteria, which helps set goals and monitor change over time.
rationale: Criterion-referenced information can clarify skill mastery and treatment targets, but technical quality and ecological relevance still matter.
choiceRationales: Ranking against a norm group describes norm-referenced testing; criterion-referenced tools compare performance with a defined standard.
Clinician-made criteria still need consistent scoring and agreement evidence, so reliability remains important for interpreting change.
Mastery on a structured task does not prove carryover, so generalization must be measured separately in natural communication contexts.
Correct. Criterion-referenced information can clarify skill mastery and treatment targets, but technical quality and ecological relevance still matter.

prompt: What should an oral-mechanism examination contribute to an evaluation?
choices: It describes structure, symmetry, range, coordination, and subsystem function to guide hypotheses and referral.
It replaces connected-speech sampling, because structural findings are sufficient to rate intelligibility in conversation.
It establishes each neurologic diagnosis independently, so a medical evaluation is not needed after the screening.
It measures receptive vocabulary by asking the person to point to pictured objects while performing oral movements.
rationale: An oral-mechanism examination contributes focused structural and functional evidence but must be integrated with task performance and other findings.
choiceRationales: Correct. An oral-mechanism examination contributes focused structural and functional evidence but must be integrated with task performance and other findings.
Structural observations cannot show how speech sounds in real use, so connected speech must still be sampled and analyzed.
The exam can raise concerns that warrant referral, but neurologic diagnosis belongs to qualified medical professionals and testing.
Receptive vocabulary is a language skill measured with separate tools; the oral-mechanism exam examines the speech and swallowing structures.

prompt: Which language-sample practice produces the most interpretable evidence?
choices: A single memorized sentence repeated several times, so that transcription is fast and scoring is highly consistent.
Adequate samples across partners and contexts, transcribed consistently and analyzed for form, content, and use.
A total word count calculated without reference to context, intelligibility, or the communicative purpose of the talk.
A sample collected in the person’s weaker language, excluding the stronger language to keep the analysis simpler.
rationale: Representative samples reveal communication in use and complement standardized, dynamic, observational, and stakeholder evidence.
choiceRationales: A memorized sentence does not show spontaneous formulation, vocabulary, or discourse, so it yields little interpretable language evidence.
Correct. Representative samples reveal communication in use and complement standardized, dynamic, observational, and stakeholder evidence.
Raw word counts ignore meaning, intelligibility, and purpose, which are needed to judge whether language is functional for the speaker.
Leaving out the stronger language underestimates true ability and can make a language difference look like a language disorder.

prompt: What is the strongest final step in diagnostic reasoning?
choices: List every obtained score in a table and let the team draw its own conclusions without a written interpretation.
Select the most severe single test result and treat it as the decisive finding for the diagnostic conclusion.
Integrate converging and conflicting evidence, state uncertainty, and make collaborative recommendations or referrals.
Set aside findings that conflict with the initial hypothesis so the report presents one consistent and persuasive picture.
rationale: Integrated reasoning connects data to function, context, differential hypotheses, limitations, person priorities, and actionable next steps.
choiceRationales: Scores without interpretation leave the referral questions unanswered and shift the clinical reasoning burden onto other team members.
One extreme score may reflect fatigue, error, or task demands, so it should be weighed against the rest of the evidence collected.
Correct. Integrated reasoning connects data to function, context, differential hypotheses, limitations, person priorities, and actionable next steps.
Ignoring disconfirming data creates confirmation bias; conflicting findings should be explained or acknowledged as remaining uncertainty.

prompt: Which evidence best distinguishes an articulation error from a phonological-pattern difficulty?
choices: The child’s chronological age compared with a single published age-of-mastery chart for each individual sound.
The number of correctly spelled words on a classroom spelling test given during the same week as the evaluation.
Ratings from a perceptual voice scale describing pitch, loudness, and quality during sustained vowel production.
Consistency across sound classes, word positions, contrasts, stimulability, and motor or structural findings.
rationale: Speech-sound assessment integrates single-word and connected-speech data, pattern analysis, motor and structural status, hearing, language, and context.
choiceRationales: Age norms show whether an error is expected, but they cannot reveal whether errors follow phonological patterns or motor limits.
Spelling reflects orthographic knowledge and instruction, so it does not distinguish articulation errors from phonological patterns.
Voice ratings describe laryngeal and resonance qualities, which are separate from the speech-sound error patterns being compared.
Correct. Speech-sound assessment integrates single-word and connected-speech data, pattern analysis, motor and structural status, hearing, language, and context.

prompt: Why assess stimulability during a speech-sound evaluation?
choices: It shows whether the sound can be elicited with models or cues, informing prognosis and target selection.
It shows whether the child has normal peripheral hearing across the speech frequencies needed for perception.
It shows whether the child understands the vocabulary used in the picture-naming probes and directions.
It shows whether the sound is already mastered in spontaneous conversation with peers at home and at school.
rationale: Stimulability is one part of a broader profile and can show response to cueing without proving generalization or diagnosis.
choiceRationales: Correct. Stimulability is one part of a broader profile and can show response to cueing without proving generalization or diagnosis.
Hearing status requires audiologic screening or evaluation; imitating a sound with cues does not establish normal peripheral hearing.
Vocabulary comprehension is a separate language question, and stimulability probes usually rely on imitation rather than word knowledge.
Stimulability examines production with models and cues, while conversational mastery is measured through spontaneous speech samples instead.

prompt: What should a comprehensive fluency assessment include beyond stuttering frequency?
choices: A count of words spoken per minute during reading aloud, used as the single indicator of overall stuttering severity.
Disfluency types and duration, tension, secondary behaviors, avoidance, emotional impact, participation, and goals.
The listener’s overall severity rating, collected once in the clinic, as the main description of the stuttering.
A detailed family history of stuttering, which determines the treatment approach and expected rate of recovery.
rationale: The lived impact of stuttering or cluttering can be substantial even when observable frequency is low in one context. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Speaking rate in one reading task misses the speaker’s experience, avoidance, and variability across real communication situations.

Correct. The lived impact of stuttering or cluttering can be substantial even when observable frequency is low in one context. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
A single listener rating omits the speaker’s own perspective and the cognitive, emotional, and participation effects of stuttering.
Family history may inform risk and counseling, but it does not describe current behaviors, impact, or the person’s treatment goals.

prompt: Before behavioral voice treatment, why is laryngoscopy or stroboscopy often important?
choices: It confirms that dysphonia is caused by poor hydration, so treatment can focus on increasing daily water intake.
It is optional, because forceful vocal exercises can begin safely before any physician examination of the vocal folds.
It allows medical review of laryngeal structure and function so treatment fits the condition and contraindications.
It is unnecessary when an experienced clinician can identify the specific lesion from auditory voice quality.
rationale: Perceptual voice quality does not uniquely identify pathology; medical and SLP evaluation support safe differential management.
choiceRationales: Hydration is one contributor to voice health, but dysphonia has many causes, including lesions and neurologic or malignant conditions.
Starting intensive exercise before an examination risks worsening an undiagnosed lesion or delaying identification of serious disease.
Correct. Perceptual voice quality does not uniquely identify pathology; medical and SLP evaluation support safe differential management.
Similar-sounding voices can arise from different laryngeal conditions, so perceptual quality alone cannot identify the specific lesion.

prompt: Which task set best supports differential motor-speech assessment?
choices: Written spelling of dictated words and sentences, used to infer motor planning from errors in letter sequences.
Pure-tone hearing screening at several frequencies, interpreted as the main evidence for the motor-speech profile.
A single sustained vowel recorded once, analyzed for duration as the complete measure of motor-speech control.
Oral motor tasks, sustained phonation, alternating and sequential motion rates, connected speech, and prosody.
rationale: Motor-speech assessment samples subsystem performance, consistency, rate, prosody, task effects, and functional communication.
choiceRationales: Spelling errors reflect literacy and orthographic knowledge, so they cannot reveal the speech subsystem patterns that separate disorders.
Hearing screening rules out a sensory contributor, but it provides no information about speech motor planning or execution.
One vowel samples phonation briefly and misses articulation, rate, sequencing, and prosody needed for differential diagnosis.
Correct. Motor-speech assessment samples subsystem performance, consistency, rate, prosody, task effects, and functional communication.

prompt: Which feature is more characteristic of apraxia of speech than dysarthria?
choices: Inconsistent sound errors and visible groping that increase with word length, reflecting impaired motor planning.
Consistent distortions across speaking tasks caused by reduced muscle strength and tone in the speech subsystems.
A purely sensory hearing loss that limits perception of speech sounds and leads to substitution errors in words.
A developmental receptive-language delay that limits understanding of directions during repetition and imitation tasks.
rationale: Apraxia often shows effortful initiation, inconsistent distortions, segmentation, and prosodic disruption; differential diagnosis uses converging tasks.
choiceRationales: Correct. Apraxia often shows effortful initiation, inconsistent distortions, segmentation, and prosodic disruption; differential diagnosis uses converging tasks.
Consistent distortions linked to weakness or abnormal tone describe dysarthria, which reflects neuromuscular execution rather than planning.
Hearing loss can affect speech perception and production, but it is a sensory problem rather than a disorder of speech motor planning.
Receptive-language delay concerns understanding meaning, so it does not explain the groping and sequencing errors of apraxia of speech.

prompt: How should resonance assessment distinguish anatomical from compensatory contributions?
choices: Treat every resonance-related error as a phonological contrast problem and target minimal pairs in therapy.
Assess oral structure and velopharyngeal function with team referral while separately analyzing learned articulation.
Assume that surgical repair will correct compensatory articulation patterns without follow-up speech therapy or monitoring.
Use a receptive vocabulary test as the sole measure for deciding whether velopharyngeal function is adequate.
rationale: Structural resonance impairment and compensatory speech behaviors can coexist and require coordinated but distinct management.
choiceRationales: Hypernasality or nasal emission may reflect structural inadequacy, which minimal-pair contrast work by itself is not able to correct.
Correct. Structural resonance impairment and compensatory speech behaviors can coexist and require coordinated but distinct management.
Compensatory articulation is learned and often persists after surgery, so it typically requires its own assessment and speech treatment.
Vocabulary knowledge says nothing about velopharyngeal closure, which instead requires perceptual, structural, and often instrumental assessment.

prompt: Why collect connected-speech samples across speaking conditions?
choices: A single-word naming test is sufficient, so a normal score there shows that no connected-speech impairment exists.
Maximum repetition rate on syllables predicts conversational intelligibility well enough to replace speech samples.
Comparing conversation, narrative, rate, loudness, fatigue, and listener context shows where function breaks down.
Partner and teacher reports are subjective, so samples should be scored in a quiet clinic room without considering them.
rationale: Task demands and context influence speech, voice, fluency, and motor performance; functional sampling reveals patterns not captured by isolated words.
choiceRationales: Single-word accuracy can be intact while longer utterances break down with added complexity, rate, or fatigue in real conversation.
Diadochokinetic rates sample motor speed, but they do not capture how intelligibility changes across tasks, partners, and settings.
Correct. Task demands and context influence speech, voice, fluency, and motor performance; functional sampling reveals patterns not captured by isolated words.
Partner reports reveal how speech works in daily environments, which clinic-only samples may miss or underestimate significantly.

prompt: Which evidence best differentiates receptive from expressive language difficulty?
choices: Tongue and lip strength ratings from an oral-mechanism exam, used to estimate how well the person follows directions.
Swallow timing on thin liquids, interpreted as an indicator of how quickly the person processes spoken sentences.
Pure-tone thresholds used as the sole language measure, because hearing level determines comprehension directly.
Comprehension across tasks and contexts compared with formulation, grammar, vocabulary, and narrative production.
rationale: Receptive and expressive processes interact but require multiple tasks and functional samples to describe the pattern accurately.
choiceRationales: Oral strength relates to speech and swallowing mechanics, so it cannot show whether someone understands or formulates language.
Swallow timing reflects oropharyngeal physiology and gives no information about how efficiently a person processes spoken language.
Hearing affects access to language, but thresholds alone cannot separate comprehension difficulties from expressive language difficulties.
Correct. Receptive and expressive processes interact but require multiple tasks and functional samples to describe the pattern accurately.

prompt: What makes social-communication assessment ecologically valid?
choices: Observation across authentic partners, settings, purposes, discourse demands, and cultural expectations.
A single decontextualized vocabulary item scored correct or incorrect in a quiet testing room with the examiner.
The examiner’s impression after one session, recorded without input from family members, teachers, or peers.
Articulation accuracy in conversation, because intelligible speech shows that social communication is intact.
rationale: Pragmatic performance varies with partner, context, power, sensory load, language background, and task expectations. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
choiceRationales: Correct. Pragmatic performance varies with partner, context, power, sensory load, language background, and task expectations. This response best integrates the person’s communication or swallowing needs, relevant physiology and evidence, professional scope, safety, participation, and appropriate follow-up.
An isolated vocabulary response removes the partners, purposes, and cues that social communication depends on in everyday life.
One examiner’s brief impression misses how the person communicates with familiar partners and across varied daily settings.
Clear speech can coexist with real difficulty in turn-taking, inference, and conversational repair, so articulation is not a proxy.

prompt: Which approach best evaluates cognitive-communication after brain injury?
choices: Conclude that no disorder is present when the person passes a brief orientation screen administered at bedside.
Assess functional attention, memory, executive function, discourse, and self-monitoring in realistic demands.
Measure tongue strength and range of motion as the primary index of cognitive recovery after the brain injury.
Administer an infant language scale, because brain injury returns adult communication to early developmental stages.
rationale: Brief tests can miss complex real-world demands; assessment should connect cognitive processes with meaningful communication and daily tasks.
choiceRationales: Brief screens often miss higher-level deficits in attention and executive function that emerge during complex everyday tasks.
Correct. Brief tests can miss complex real-world demands; assessment should connect cognitive processes with meaningful communication and daily tasks.
Tongue strength concerns oral motor function and does not measure the attention, memory, or reasoning skills affected by injury.
Adults with brain injury keep prior knowledge and need age-appropriate functional measures rather than tools normed for infants.

prompt: What is feature matching in an AAC assessment?
choices: Choosing the device with the largest stored vocabulary, since more words will benefit every AAC user equally.
Requiring evidence that speech therapy has failed before considering any AAC system, including low-tech supports.
Aligning the person’s needs, access methods, abilities, partners, and settings to specific system features.
Selecting a system from a catalog description without device trials or input from communication partners.
rationale: AAC selection is individualized and iterative; trials, communication opportunities, partner support, and changing needs shape recommendations.
choiceRationales: A very large vocabulary can overwhelm some users or require access skills they lack, so vocabulary size must fit the person.
Current practice rejects readiness or failure prerequisites; AAC can support speech and language development from the start.
Correct. AAC selection is individualized and iterative; trials, communication opportunities, partner support, and changing needs shape recommendations.
Trials and partner input reveal whether access, symbols, and portability actually work in daily life, which a catalog cannot show.

prompt: Which hearing information is most relevant to communication assessment?
choices: The unaided pure-tone average alone, since one number summarizes how the person hears speech in every setting.
The style and color of the hearing device, which predict how consistently a child will wear it in the classroom.
The child’s articulation score, which reflects auditory access more accurately than an audiologic evaluation.
Audiologic configuration, aided access, device use, listening environments, and language exposure and mode.
rationale: Communication access depends on hearing status, technology, environment, linguistic experience, visual supports, and individual response.
choiceRationales: An unaided average hides configuration, aided benefit, and noisy-room performance, all of which shape communication access.
Device appearance may matter to the child socially, but it does not describe auditory access, consistency of use, or language exposure.
Articulation can be affected by hearing, but it is an indirect outcome and cannot replace audiologic information about access.
Correct. Communication access depends on hearing status, technology, environment, linguistic experience, visual supports, and individual response.

prompt: How should a bilingual language evaluation use evidence across languages?
choices: Assess all relevant languages with qualified support using history, samples, and dynamic methods, noting limits.
Translate an English norm-referenced test and report the standard score as though the norms still applied.
Assess English proficiency alone, regardless of the person’s exposure history or use of other languages at home.
Score dialect features as errors, because they differ from the general American English forms in the test manual.
rationale: Disorder should be supported by converging difficulty across languages or learning contexts, not difference or limited exposure alone.
choiceRationales: Correct. Disorder should be supported by converging difficulty across languages or learning contexts, not difference or limited exposure alone.
Translation changes item difficulty and content, so the original norms no longer apply and the standard score is not valid.
Testing one language can underestimate total language ability and confuse typical second-language learning with a disorder.
Dialect features are rule-governed variations, and counting them as errors leads to overidentification of language disorder.

prompt: Why assess reading and writing in a school-age language evaluation?
choices: Literacy falls outside SLP scope, so reading tasks are included to document teacher concerns for the record.
Spoken and written language share vocabulary, syntax, and phonological foundations that affect curriculum access.
A reading difficulty confirms a motor-speech disorder, so oral reading is used to diagnose dysarthria or apraxia.
Handwriting speed is the most relevant literacy measure because it predicts language performance across subjects.
rationale: Language and literacy are interconnected; assessment should coordinate with educators and consider educational impact and role boundaries.
choiceRationales: Professional guidance places spoken and written language within SLP roles, especially where language weaknesses affect literacy.
Correct. Language and literacy are interconnected; assessment should coordinate with educators and consider educational impact and role boundaries.
Reading problems usually reflect language or phonological factors, and a motor-speech diagnosis requires a dedicated speech motor assessment.
Handwriting speed is mainly a fine-motor skill and does not capture the language foundations that support reading and writing.

prompt: Which profile is consistent with aphasia assessment rather than a single naming test?
choices: Speech sound accuracy in single words, since aphasia is defined by articulation errors on a picture-naming test.
Swallowing physiology during a bedside evaluation, because language deficits after stroke reflect oral weakness.
Comprehension, expression, naming, repetition, reading, writing, discourse, and functional participation.
One confrontation-naming score, treated as the complete diagnosis and severity rating for the language disorder.
rationale: Aphasia is multimodal and variable; comprehensive assessment identifies strengths, barriers, supports, and meaningful communication priorities.
choiceRationales: Aphasia is a language disorder across modalities; articulation errors point more toward motor-speech involvement than aphasia.
Swallowing problems may co-occur after stroke, but they do not measure comprehension, formulation, or other language modalities.
Correct. Aphasia is multimodal and variable; comprehensive assessment identifies strengths, barriers, supports, and meaningful communication priorities.
Naming is one useful task, yet aphasia profiles require comprehension, repetition, discourse, literacy, and functional measures.

prompt: What is the purpose of a clinical swallowing evaluation?
choices: Directly visualize each pharyngeal event, including laryngeal penetration and residue, without instrumental tools.
Rule out silent aspiration with certainty, since a strong cough during trials confirms that the airway is protected.
Replace the medical and nutritional assessment by determining calorie needs and diet orders from bedside trials.
Integrate history, alertness, oral and cranial-nerve findings, trials when appropriate, risk, and need for referral.
rationale: Clinical evaluation identifies patterns and risk but cannot directly visualize swallowing physiology or exclude silent aspiration.
choiceRationales: Pharyngeal events such as penetration and residue cannot be seen at bedside; visualizing them requires an instrumental study.
Silent aspiration produces no cough, so bedside trials cannot exclude it, and a strong cough does not prove airway protection.
Clinical swallowing findings inform the team, but medical and nutritional assessment remain the roles of physicians and dietitians.
Correct. Clinical evaluation identifies patterns and risk but cannot directly visualize swallowing physiology or exclude silent aspiration.

prompt: Which instrumental exam uses dynamic radiography to examine bolus flow through oral, pharyngeal, and upper-esophageal swallowing events?
choices: A videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS), performed with appropriate team and radiation-safety considerations.
A single static chest radiograph taken after the meal to look for signs of aspiration in the lower lungs.
Fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing, which views the pharynx through a nasally passed endoscope.
High-resolution manometry, which measures pharyngeal and esophageal pressures with a catheter rather than images.
rationale: VFSS provides dynamic radiographic information about bolus flow and physiology and can test selected strategies under study conditions.
choiceRationales: Correct. VFSS provides dynamic radiographic information about bolus flow and physiology and can test selected strategies under study conditions.
A static chest film may show later lung changes, but it does not capture bolus movement through the swallow as it happens.
FEES is a valuable instrumental study, but it uses endoscopic video rather than radiography and has a white-out at the swallow.
Manometry records pressure data along the pharynx and esophagus, so it does not provide radiographic images of bolus flow.

prompt: Which statement accurately identifies a major advantage of FEES?
choices: VFSS continuously displays pharyngeal swallowing with no white-out period and without any ionizing radiation.
FEES is portable and can assess anatomy, secretions, fatigue, and repeated trials without ionizing radiation.
Pure-tone audiometry directly visualizes laryngeal anatomy and bolus flow during each swallow at the bedside.
FEES directly images the oral preparatory phase and the upper esophagus throughout the entirety of every swallow.
rationale: FEES offers portable endoscopic assessment of relevant anatomy and swallowing before and after the brief white-out period.
choiceRationales: VFSS uses fluoroscopy, which involves radiation exposure, and the white-out period is a limitation of FEES rather than VFSS.
Correct. FEES offers portable endoscopic assessment of relevant anatomy and swallowing before and after the brief white-out period.
Audiometry measures hearing thresholds and provides no view of laryngeal structures or the movement of a bolus.
The endoscope sits above the larynx, so FEES does not show the oral phase or esophagus and loses the view during the swallow.

prompt: Why can aspiration be missed during a clinical swallow examination?
choices: An absence of coughing during trials proves that the airway was protected on each swallow that was observed.
